messages.subject: explanation of half-Cauchy variance prior
parts:
Hi all,

I have a random effect with fewer than 5 levels and I'm interested in using a half-Cauchy distribution for the prior on the variance, following recommendations by Gelman (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf). Gelman formulates the half-Cauchy in a model like this:

model {
    for (j in 1:J) { # J = the number of schools
        y[j] ~ dnorm (theta[j], tau.y[j]) # data model: the likelihood
        theta[j] <- mu.theta + xi*eta[j]
        tau.y[j] <- pow(sigma.y[j], -2)
    }
    xi ~ dnorm (0, tau.xi)
    tau.xi <- pow(prior.scale, -2)
    for (j in 1:J) {
        eta[j] ~ dnorm (0, tau.eta) # hierarchical model for theta
    }
    tau.eta ~ dgamma (.5, .5) # chi^2 with 1 d.f.
    sigma.theta <- abs(xi)/sqrt(tau.eta) # cauchy = normal/sqrt(chi^2)
    mu.theta ~ dnorm (0.0, 1.0E-6) # noninformative prior on mu
}

I was wondering if anyone could provide some explanation for how the half-Cauchy is being induced here and what the parameters are representing - in particular "xi" and "sigma.theta" (scale and location of the half-Cauchy?). Can "sigma.theta" be interpreted as the standard deviation for the random effects and, for example, compared directly with a s.d. estimate using a uniform prior? For example, could it be directly compared to "sd.eta" in:

model {

...

    for (j in 1:J) {
        eta[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.eta)
    }
    tau.eta <- pow(sd.eta, -2)
    sd.eta ~ dunif(0, 10)

...

}

Thanks,
Ollie
